newsitem.title: INDIA: Tiger doomed unless India acts fast -wildlife group.
newsitem.headline: Tiger doomed unless India acts fast -wildlife group.

text.p: India, home to 60 percent of the world's surviving tigers, must act swiftly to crack down on poaching to save the species from rapid extinction, an international wildlife protection group said on Thursday.
"If there is any chance of saving the tiger in the world, it is here in India, its last stronghold," London-based Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA) director Dave Currey told a news conference.
"But political apathy and inaction has left the Indian tiger unprotected and increasingly under poaching pressure," he said.
At least one of India's estimated 2,500 tigers is killed every day to feed a lucrative international trade in tiger bones, skins, nails, teeth and penises, Currey said.
"Yet, there hasn't been a recognition of an emergency, and this needs to be dealt with with an emergency action plan, with resources," he said.
The EIA says the tiger faces extinction within a decade.
Indian Environment Minister Saifuddin Soz last week said rich nations must also shoulder the responsibility of conserving seriously endangered species like the tiger.

"Most Asian countries with tiger populations are faced with a dilemma. We are charged with the responsibility of conserving them, yet on account of the increasing demands of growing populations, we are under pressure to step up developmental activities," Soz said.
India in 1972 launched a tiger preservation programme, called Project Tiger, designating protected areas as tiger sanctuaries and imposing bans on their hunting and trade.
But when the tiger virtually disappeared from the forests of China in the 1980s, Chinese hunters turned to the rich stock of neighbouring India, the EIA said.
It said China remained the primary destination for tiger parts, commonly used in traditional medicines. The tiger is now found in the wild in only 14 countries.

"It is true that saving the tiger is the responsibility of the consuming country," Currey said, citing proposed U.S. laws to deal with widespread sales of Chinese-made tiger products in U.S. drug stores and supermarkets.
"But then, we wouldn't tell people who are running away with our children just to stop -- we would protect our children as well. The word has to come from India," he said.
